      "paper_id": "manual-e4d6ad7ca1",
      "title": "Anaphoric Annotation in the ARRAU Corpus",
      "research_question": "How can a corpus annotation scheme represent ambiguous anaphora, plural or multiple antecedents, and discourse-deictic reference to abstract entities while maintaining measurable annotation reliability?",
      "methodology": "The authors developed the ARRAU annotation scheme iteratively through annotation experiments, mostly using MMAX2, with multiple annotators and Krippendorff's alpha to assess reliability. They then applied the scheme to task-oriented dialogue, spoken narrative, mixed-domain text, and Wall Street Journal material. The scheme marks noun phrases as possible nominal antecedents, clauses as possible discourse-deictic antecedents, and uses separate pointer sets to distinguish plural antecedents from genuinely ambiguous alternatives.",
      "key_findings": [
        {
          "finding": "ARRAU explicitly distinguishes plural expressions with multiple antecedents from ambiguous expressions with alternative antecedent interpretations.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "4.2 Annotation scheme"
        },
        {
          "finding": "The scheme permits an anaphoric expression to point to a clause that introduces an event, action, or plan, rather than requiring every antecedent to be a noun phrase.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "4.2 Annotation scheme"
        },
        {
          "finding": "Agreement on anaphoric chains was approximately alpha 0.6-0.7, while agreement for discourse-deictic antecedent regions was lower at approximately alpha 0.55 because annotators often disagreed about exact textual boundaries.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "3. Agreement on ambiguity and discourse deixis"
        },
        {
          "finding": "Annotators often failed to mark ambiguity explicitly, but ambiguity could frequently be detected from different annotators independently selecting different antecedents for the same expression.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "3. Agreement on ambiguity and discourse deixis"
        },
        {
          "finding": "The reported corpus contained 110 texts, 24,321 markables, 455 markables pointing to discourse regions, and 103 expressions explicitly marked as ambiguous.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "4.1 Composition"
        },
        {
          "finding": "A preliminary resolver that required equivalence classes could not preserve the full ambiguity representation and instead selected the first annotated interpretation of ambiguous anaphors.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "5. Preliminary experiments"
        }
      ],
      "limitations": [
        "Agreement remained only moderate for ordinary anaphoric chains and was lower for the exact boundaries of discourse-deictic antecedents.",
        "The corpus composition described in the paper was still evolving, with additional material planned for the final version.",
        "The preliminary resolution experiment collapsed ambiguous alternatives to a single interpretation because its representation assumed equivalence classes.",
        "Potential noun phrases and clauses were initially identified automatically and then corrected manually, creating a labor-intensive preprocessing dependency.",
        "The paper concerns anaphoric reference rather than explicit question-to-reply alignment, so it does not directly quantify partial answers, unanswered questions, or email reply behavior.",
        "The paper states that a first release had been completed but only expresses an intention to make it publicly available, so public dataset availability is not established by the source read."

        "ambiguity_from_annotator_disagreement": 0.98,
        "corpus_statistics": 0.99,
        "equivalence_model_loses_ambiguity": 0.98
      },
      "raw_claims": [
        "ARRAU was designed to cover forms of anaphora that are poorly represented in conventional coreference corpora.",
        "Its annotation scheme allows more than one antecedent pointer for a single anaphoric expression.",
        "Separate pointer sets distinguish alternative interpretations from plural reference to several antecedents.",
        "Clauses are available as antecedents for references to abstract discourse entities.",
        "Human agreement was substantially affected by uncertainty about the boundaries of discourse-deictic antecedents.",
        "Disagreement among annotators can itself provide evidence that an expression is ambiguous.",
        "The reported corpus combines dialogue, narrative, newspaper, and mixed-domain texts.",
        "The reported release contains 455 discourse-region references and 103 explicitly ambiguous markables.",
        "Treating coreference solely as an equivalence relation cannot faithfully retain all of ARRAU's ambiguity annotations."

      "source_url": "https://www.researchgate.net/publication/220745830_Anaphoric_Annotation_in_the_ARRAU_Corpus",
      "access": "full_text"
    },

      "paper_id": "manual-1e515febba",
      "title": "Resolving Discourse Deictic Anaphora in Dialogues",
      "research_question": "Can discourse-deictic pronouns and demonstratives in spoken dialogue be classified and resolved to clausal or multi-clause antecedents using dialogue-act structure, common-ground constraints, and antecedent compatibility?",
      "methodology": "The authors developed a rule-based discourse-deictic anaphora resolver using Switchboard telephone conversations, dialogue-act segmentation, anaphor-type classification, semantic compatibility constraints, and ranked discourse contexts. Five randomly selected dialogues were annotated by the two authors, with two used to develop the annotation procedure and three used for testing. A reconciled manual annotation served as the evaluation key for antecedent resolution.",
      "key_findings": [
        {
          "finding": "Only 45.1% of the examined anaphoric references had ordinary individual NP antecedents, whereas 22.6% were discourse-deictic references to non-NP material such as VPs, sentences, or strings of sentences.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "2. Anaphor Types in Dialogues"
        },
        {
          "finding": "The paper explicitly treats sentences and strings of sentences as possible antecedents, providing an empirical basis for multi-proposition antecedent resolution in dialogue.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "2. Anaphor Types in Dialogues"

        {
          "finding": "Dialogue-act labels achieved aggregate kappa 0.8708, while classification of pronouns and demonstratives achieved kappas 0.8055 and 0.7985 respectively.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "5.1 Annotation"

          "finding": "For manually identifying antecedents of agreed discourse-deictic anaphors, annotator accuracy against the reconciled key ranged from 85.7% to 94.3%.",

          "finding": "The discourse-deictic resolution algorithm achieved 63.6% precision and 70% recall on the three test dialogues.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "5.2 Evaluation of the Algorithm"
        },
        {
          "finding": "A major source of errors was confusing vague anaphors with discourse-deictic anaphors because the surrounding context usually supplied some apparently compatible antecedent.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "5.2 Evaluation of the Algorithm"
        },

          "finding": "The model uses acknowledgments and dialogue-act structure to determine what discourse material has entered common ground, and it explicitly addresses abandoned or partial utterances as a spoken-dialogue problem.",

          "section": "1. Introduction and 3. Synchronising Units"
        }

        "The evaluation used only five Switchboard dialogues, of which only three were test dialogues.",

        "The resolver does not provide a general model of question-answer alignment or explicitly measure unanswered or partially answered questions.",

      "raw_claims": [
        "Discourse-deictic anaphora are common enough in Switchboard that an NP-only resolver would leave a substantial portion of anaphoric references untreated.",
        "Discourse-deictic antecedents can be verbal phrases, whole sentences, or sequences of sentences.",
        "Spoken dialogue contains partial and self-repaired utterances that cannot simply be discarded from the discourse model.",
        "The approach segments dialogue pragmatically rather than relying on punctuation-defined sentences.",
        "Acknowledgments are used as evidence that conversational material has entered common ground.",
        "Pronoun and demonstrative anaphor types could be classified with approximately 0.8 kappa agreement.",
        "Human annotators located discourse-deictic antecedents with 85.7% to 94.3% accuracy relative to their reconciled annotation.",
        "The resolver obtained 63.6% precision and 70% recall.",
        "Vague references were a prominent source of false discourse-deictic resolutions."

      "source_url": "https://aclanthology.org/E99-1006.pdf",
      "access": "full_text"
    },

      "paper_id": "manual-14f72b0c0b",
      "title": "Discourse Structure and Dialogue Acts in Multiparty Dialogue: the STAC Corpus",
      "research_question": "How can full discourse structure in multi-party strategic chat be annotated so that interleaved threads, partial or indirect answers, multiple replies, and multi-unit discourse arguments are represented faithfully?",
      "methodology": "The authors constructed STAC from online Settlers of Catan games, aligning player chat with game events and annotating elementary discourse units, discourse-relation attachments, dialogue acts, and complex discourse units under SDRT. Four non-expert annotators were trained, doubly annotated material was used to measure agreement, and experts performed multiple revision passes. The paper also analyzes structural statistics and simple attachment baselines to characterize how multi-party dialogue differs from monologic text.",
      "key_findings": [
        {
          "finding": "The corpus contains cases where one question receives several distinct replies and one subsequent acknowledgment simultaneously targets all of those replies, directly motivating a graph rather than a tree representation.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "2. Discourse Structure"
        },
        {
          "finding": "The Question-Answer Pair relation explicitly includes partial and indirect answers, so reply alignment is not restricted to complete direct answers.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "2. Discourse Structure"
        },
        {
          "finding": "Complex discourse units group multiple EDUs or other CDUs so that a multi-proposition span can function as a single argument of another discourse relation.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "2. Discourse Structure"
        },
        {
          "finding": "The reported corpus contains 1,081 dialogues, 10,678 EDUs, 10,513 discourse-relation instances, and 1,284 complex discourse units.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "3. Details on the Annotation Process"
        },
        {
          "finding": "Question-Answer Pair is the most frequent relation in the reported corpus, with 2,541 instances out of 10,513 relation instances.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "4. Corpus Statistics and Comparison"
        },
        {
          "finding": "Inter-annotator agreement was kappa 0.72 for attachment structure and 0.58 for relation labeling on doubly annotated dialogues.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "3. Details on the Annotation Process"
        },
        {
          "finding": "A LAST-attachment baseline achieved 60.2% precision, 56.6% recall, and 58.4% F1 globally, with poorer results between different speakers, supporting the prevalence of non-local attachments in multi-party dialogue.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "4. Corpus Statistics and Comparison"
        },
        {
          "finding": "Even with oracle local attachment and labeling information, MST decoding missed 9% of correct attachments, demonstrating an empirical limitation of forcing the discourse graph into a tree.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "5. Experimentation"
        }
      ],
      "limitations": [
        "The corpus is drawn from a competitive Settlers of Catan environment, so discourse behavior may not generalize directly to workplace email or other dialogue domains.",

        "Automatic EDU segmentation was manually corrected, adding expert labor and potential preprocessing dependence.",
        "The corpus represents answered, partial, and indirect Question-Answer Pair relations but does not provide a dedicated empirical category for every question that receives no answer.",
        "Dependency-style parsing experiments simplify the richer SDRT representation and therefore do not preserve every complex discourse unit directly."

      },
      "raw_claims": [
        "STAC represents multi-party chat as discourse graphs rather than assuming that each contribution has only one tree parent.",
        "A corpus example contains three negative replies to one question and an acknowledgment linked to all three replies.",
        "Question-Answer Pair annotations include partial and indirect answers.",
        "Follow-up questions can be represented with a separate Question-Elaboration relation.",
        "Complex discourse units allow several elementary contributions to behave as one discourse argument.",
        "The reported release includes 1,284 complex discourse units.",
        "Question-Answer Pair is the most frequent annotated relation in the reported corpus.",
        "Attachment agreement was higher than discourse-relation label agreement.",
        "Simple attachment to the immediately preceding EDU performs worse in multi-party dialogue than the comparison reported for monologic text.",
        "Tree-constrained MST decoding cannot reproduce all gold discourse attachments even when supplied with oracle local information."
      ],
      "source_url": "https://aclanthology.org/L16-1432.pdf",
      "access": "full_text"
    },

      "paper_id": "doi-10-1007-s10489-013-0481-1",
      "title": "Towards identifying unresolved discussions in student online forums",
      "research_question": "Can forum speech acts and thread-level discourse structures be used to identify student discussions containing confusion, unanswered questions, or otherwise unresolved issues?",
      "methodology": "The paper defines forum speech acts representing message roles such as questions, issue raising, and answers, and then models thread-level structures such as whether a question receives an answer.       "key_findings": [
        {
          "finding": "The approach explicitly models whether a question in a threaded discussion was replied to with an answer.",

          "section": "Abstract"

          "finding": "The modeled discourse structures are used to identify threads containing unanswered questions or unresolved issues rather than relying only on isolated message classification.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",

          "finding": "The reported discussion-thread classifiers achieved accuracies ranging from 0.79 to 0.87 across several classification problems.",

      "raw_claims": [
        "The study targets automated identification of unresolved student online discussions.",

    {
      "paper_id": "doi-10-18653-v1-d15-1109",
      "title": "Discourse parsing for multi-party chat dialogues",
      "research_question": "How accurately can full multi-party chat discourse structure, including interleaved threads and non-tree attachment patterns, be parsed using local attachment models combined with global decoding?",
      "methodology": "The authors use the STAC Settlers of Catan corpus annotated with SDRT discourse structures and convert its hypergraphs into dependency-style structures by replacing complex discourse units with recursive heads. They train regularized maximum-entropy local attachment and relation models using positional, lexical, syntactic, and dialogue-act features, then compare local, LAST, and MST-based decoding strategies.         {
          "finding": "The corpus contains a question with three separate negative replies followed by one acknowledgment attached to all three replies, demonstrating many-to-one and one-to-many discourse alignment that cannot be represented faithfully as an ordinary tree.",

          "section": "2. What's so special about multi party dialogue?"

          "finding": "Complex discourse units can combine several contributions into one antecedent, and some observed CDUs encompass an entire question-answering session.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "2. What's so special about multi party dialogue?"
        },
        {
          "finding": "An example combines two separate proposal turns into a complex discourse unit that jointly serves as the antecedent of a conditional relation, directly illustrating a multi-proposition antecedent.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "2. What's so special about multi party dialogue?"
        },
        {
          "finding": "The dataset used for parsing contains 1,091 dialogues, 10,677 EDUs, and 11,348 discourse relations, with 968 dialogues used for training and 123 for testing.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "3. The STAC corpus"
        },
        {
          "finding": "Inter-annotator agreement for the discourse annotations was kappa 0.72 for attachment and 0.58 for relation labeling.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "3. The STAC corpus"

        {
          "finding": "The best global configuration achieved directed attachment F1 of 0.671, fully labeled structure F1 of 0.516, and undirected attachment F1 of 0.680.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "5. Results"
        },
        {
          "finding": "The LAST baseline achieved attachment F1 of 0.584 and fully labeled structure F1 of 0.391, while the local classifier achieved directed attachment F1 of 0.541 and labeled F1 of 0.446.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "5. Results"
        },
        {
          "finding": "The dependency conversion removes CDU-membership edges and replaces attachments to a CDU with attachment to its head EDU, so the parsing representation deliberately collapses some multi-proposition structure present in the original annotation.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "4. Discourse Parsing"

      "limitations": [

        "The conversion from SDRT hypergraphs to dependency graphs removes CDU-membership edges and therefore prevents the parser from directly recovering the complete original multi-proposition structure.",
